blocks.alt: Design-system components and documentation at The Adecco Group

blocks.text: The components existed. Teams stopped trusting them

The Adecco Group’s design system was widely used in Figma, but confidence fell when engineers tried to build with it. React components, Storybook examples and design files no longer matched. Accessibility problems repeatedly appeared during QA, while incomplete guidance left developers guessing how components should work together.
Under deadline pressure, product teams began creating their own versions. What looked like a collection of component defects had become a trust problem across design and engineering.

items: Version drift
Figma, Storybook and React represented different states of the same component.
Accessibility
Keyboard, ARIA and contrast issues reached product QA.
Documentation
Developers could see individual components but not how to compose them.
Communication
Teams did not know when releases happened or what a change meant for their work.

blocks.alt: Existing design-system documentation at The Adecco Group
blocks.caption: The documentation exposed individual components, but developers still lacked reliable guidance on composition, accessibility and change.

blocks.text: I became the primary driver of a four-week audit. I reviewed more than 110 React components across Figma, Storybook, documentation and production code, recording accessibility defects and mismatches in a shared audit table.

rows: Design
Does Figma represent the component accurately?
Variants, spacing, typography and states
Code
Does the React component behave as documented?
Props, interactions and implementation differences
Accessibility
Can people operate and understand it?
Keyboard behaviour, focus, roles and contrast
Governance
Can teams understand what changed?
Ownership, release notes, versioning and impact

blocks.text: I used BrowserStack, axe-core and manual WCAG checks to find issues that automated scans alone would miss. The audit became a shared view of the system rather than a private defect list, allowing product teams to see what was being fixed and why.

blocks.alt: Design-system audit showing component gaps and remediation status
blocks.caption: The audit connected each visible inconsistency to its design, code, documentation and accessibility state.

blocks.text: Sprint demos showed the practical effect of the drift. Developers were spending time setting up components, asking the design-system team for help or recreating patterns to meet delivery dates. I interviewed developers and the internal team to understand where confidence was breaking down.

items: I end up guessing how these components are meant to work together.
I spend more time setting things up than building the feature.
I never know when a release goes out or what has changed.

blocks.text: This changed the order of the work. Accessibility defects remained urgent, but repairing code alone would not restore adoption. Developers also needed clearer setup guidance and a release process they could follow without relying on someone from the design-system team.

rows: Fix keyboard, role and contrast defects
Add accessibility expectations to component guidance
Align Figma and React variants
Define which source owns each type of change
Correct spacing and typography
Review design and code together before release
Answer recurring setup questions
Create onboarding guides and short walkthroughs
Explain the current release
Publish impact-labelled release notes every two weeks

blocks.text: Fixing components was only half the work

I worked directly in the component library and Figma files, then coordinated remediation across three frontend engineers. I divided the work, checked consistency and brought unresolved design decisions back into the shared system rather than allowing product-specific fixes to remain isolated.

blocks.label: Design-system delivery
blocks.title: Component repair and governance moved together
items: Audit
Compare Figma, Storybook, React and accessibility behaviour.
Remediate
Correct implementation, states, tokens and documentation.
Verify
Re-test with BrowserStack, axe-core and manual checks.
Release
Explain the change, its impact and any migration needed.
Teach
Use demos and onboarding material to make the update usable.

blocks.text: Product teams originally wanted to create their own components to unblock delivery. I asked them to identify the highest-priority gaps, made the audit visible and opened sprint planning, demos and reviews. That transparency gave teams a way to influence the system without fragmenting it further.

The project used two operational signals: accessibility issues raised during QA and the time needed to onboard developers. After remediation, QA-reported issues fell to near zero, while onboarding fell from five days to roughly three hours. More than 110 components were reviewed and aligned across design and code.

items: Accessibility
QA-reported accessibility issues fell to near zero.
Coverage
More than 110 React components were reviewed across Figma, Storybook and code.
Onboarding
Developer ramp-up fell from five days to around three hours.

blocks.text: The outcome was not a permanently finished library. It was a design system with a clearer way to detect drift, communicate changes and prevent the same defects returning unnoticed.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.text: Teams trust a design system when its components work, but they keep trusting it when ownership, decisions and changes remain visible.
